title: Automating the analysis of micron-scale synchrotron diffraction data on inhomogeneous polycrystalline samples: a solid oxide electrolysis cell case study
authors: Liam A. V. Nagle-Cocco, Christopher A. Crain, Michael J. Dzara, Mathias A. Kiefer, Madeline G. Port, Tolga Han Ulucan, Madeline Van Winkle, Oscar Hathaway, Nicholas A. Strange
abstract: A novel approach to post mortem characterisation of electrochemical and photovoltaic devices is spatially-resolved diffraction using a hyper-focused, micron-width x-ray beam to examine the distribution of degradation products and strain, a technique called $μ$-XRD. Aside from the experimental difficulties associated with beam focusing and sample preparation, which are themselves non-trivial, the analysis of resulting data is complex and challenging, with full Rietveld analysis rarely attempted in literature. The difficulty lies in the size of the data, which may consist of hundreds or even thousands of diffraction patterns with very different crystallographic phase compositions depending on position within the device, and the difficulty in fitting the data due to the presence of many phases at the same position, including possible degradation products which may be difficult to index and assign to known phases. In this paper, we present a fully-automated open access Python routine for performing phase identification and Rietveld analysis on 2D datasets of diffraction pattern taken at micron-scale positions, measured over the cross-section of a chemically inhomogeneous device with polycrystalline phases. Solid oxide electrolyser cells are a promising technology for green hydrogen production which can utilise waste heat to split water at higher efficiencies than low-temperature electrolysis techniques such as polymer electrolyte membranes, but exhibit many degradation modes due to the high operating temperatures. We present a case study using our analysis protocol on an SOEC fragment encompassing the air electrode, cation diffusion barrier, electrolyte, and fuel electrode. With modification, this protocol could be applied to other devices such as all-solid-state batteries, wet-electrolyte battery electrodes, solid oxide fuel cells, photovoltaic devices, and metal-oxide pseudocapacitors.
summary: This paper presents a novel, fully automated computational protocol for analyzing complex, spatially-resolved X-ray diffraction data from inhomogeneous materials like SOECs. By developing an open-access Python routine, the authors overcome significant manual analysis hurdles to map phase composition and strain across device cross-sections. This methodology is valuable for post mortem characterization of high-temperature electrochemical energy devices.
main_problem: The primary challenge is automating the analysis of massive, spatially-resolved synchrotron diffraction datasets from chemically inhomogeneous polycrystalline materials.
main_result: The authors developed and applied a fully automated Python routine that successfully performs phase identification and Rietveld refinement across complex device cross-sections, enabling detailed post mortem characterization of degradation products in SOECs.
method: The method involves an iterative, automated protocol combining peak matching, goodness-of-fit checks ($	ext{R}_{	ext{wp}}/	ext{R}_{	ext{exp}}$), and scale factor analysis within a Rietveld framework, implemented via Python scripts calling Topas.
model_or_system: The study focuses on Solid Oxide Electrolyser Cells (SOECs) fragments, which are analyzed using micron-scale X-ray diffraction ($\mu$-XRD). The technique is applicable to other electrochemical devices like all-solid-state batteries and fuel cells.
key_observables: Lattice parameters of various phases ($	ext{YSZ}$, $	ext{LSCF-6428}$), phase composition maps, strain distribution, and goodness-of-fit metrics across the sample cross-section.
important_parameters: Micron beam width, operating temperatures (high for SOECs), and crystallographic parameters derived from refinement ($	ext{R}_{	ext{wp}}/	ext{R}_{	ext{exp}}$).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that the automated protocol can reliably handle data complexity; specific limitations include assuming cubic unit cells when rhombohedral structures are expected, and fixing the zero error to avoid correlation issues.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate SOEC designs, pseudo-code for the phase identification algorithm, heatmaps showing variations in lattice parameters and zero error across the sample, and plots comparing fit quality metrics.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the $\mu$-XRD technique and its analytical bottleneck. It details the automated Python routine (including pseudocode) and applies it to an SOEC case study, presenting results on phase mapping, lattice parameter variations due to chemistry/strain, and limitations encountered during refinement.
